crafts.name: Shingzo
crafts.description: Timber joinery for dzongs, temples and houses — beams, brackets and window frames cut without nails.
crafts.history:
Carpentry arrived in Bhutan with the building of the dzongs, and it is the craft the country's architecture is named for. When Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal consolidated the western valleys in the seventeenth century, he built fortress-monasteries at Simtokha, Punakha and Wangdue Phodrang, and the carpenters who raised them worked without iron. That constraint shaped everything: a beam had to lock into a post by geometry alone, so joints were cut to hold under load and to move under tremor rather than snap.

The craft was organised as one of the thirteen when Zorig Chusum was formally categorised, and the master carpenter — the zowo — held a rank close to an architect's. He set out a whole building from proportion held in memory, without drawings, and was answerable for it. Apprenticeship ran for years and was paid in keep rather than wages.

Today the trade divides. Some carpenters work on heritage restoration under the Department of Culture, where the old methods are required. Others build ordinary houses with imported timber and steel fixings. HAB's concern is the first group: there are fewer master carpenters able to set out a dzong gallery than at any point in living memory, and the skill does not survive being written down.
crafts.long_description: Shingzo is the craft that holds Bhutanese architecture together. A carpenter works without nails: beams, brackets, rafters and window frames are cut so precisely that they lock under their own load, which lets a building flex in an earthquake instead of shearing. The trade covers everything from a farmhouse roof to the great cantilevered galleries of a dzong, and a master carpenter is expected to set out a whole structure from memory and proportion rather than from drawings. A master sets out the whole frame before a single joint is cut, working from proportion rather than drawings, and is answerable for whether it stands.
crafts.technique: Mortise-and-tenon joinery cut by hand; no nails, no glue
crafts.typical_products: structural joinery, doors, window frames, brackets
crafts.shop_note: Carpentry is commissioned, not shipped. Send the secretariat your building or restoration brief and we will match it to a Shingzo member.

crafts.name: Dozo
crafts.description: Stone and rammed-earth walls, the load-bearing craft behind every dzong and farmhouse.
crafts.history:
Masonry is probably the oldest of the thirteen, and certainly the least celebrated. Bhutan's earliest surviving structures — the watchtowers and the dzong foundations — are stone, and the technique used to raise them has changed remarkably little. Walls were built in dressed stone laid dry or in mud mortar, or in rammed earth compacted inside timber shuttering by foot and mallet, lift by lift, until the wall could carry a roof.

The craft's status has always been ambiguous. A mason's work disappears the moment it is rendered and whitewashed, and unlike a painter or a silversmith he leaves no visible signature. Yet the mason decided whether a building stood. In the 1897 and 2009 earthquakes it was masonry detailing — the batter of a wall, the placement of a bond stone — that determined which structures survived.

The same skill built the mani walls and chortens along mountain paths, and the retaining walls holding terraced fields on steep ground. Both are still needed. What has changed is that concrete is faster and cheaper, so young masons learn blockwork rather than rammed earth, and the number who can build a traditional wall correctly is falling in every dzongkhag.
crafts.long_description: Dozo is the oldest of the thirteen and the least visible: once a wall is rendered and whitewashed, the craft disappears into the building. Masons work in dressed stone and in rammed earth, raising walls in lifts inside timber shuttering and compacting each layer by foot and mallet. The same skill builds the mani walls and chortens that mark a mountain path, and the retaining walls that keep terraced fields from sliding. A wall is judged by its batter and its bond stones, both invisible once rendered, and both what decides whether it survives a tremor.
crafts.technique: Dressed stone laid dry or in mud mortar; rammed earth in timber shuttering
crafts.materials: River stone, quarried stone, subsoil, timber shuttering
crafts.typical_products: stone and rammed-earth walling, paving, mani walls, chortens
crafts.shop_note: Masonry is commissioned on site. Send the secretariat your construction or heritage-repair brief and we will match it to a Dozo member.

crafts.name: Parzo
crafts.description: Carving in wood, slate and stone: masks, altar panels, printing blocks and mani walls.
crafts.history:
Carving is the craft that made Bhutanese Buddhism portable. Before paper presses arrived, scripture was published from woodblocks — text cut in mirror image into seasoned wood, inked and pressed onto desho paper, sheet by sheet. Whole libraries at Punakha and Trongsa were produced this way, and a single mistake in a block meant recutting it.

The same trade cut the masks worn in the tshechu dances, the choesham panels of household altars, and the deep relief on temple facades. In slate, it produced the carved plaques set into mani walls along mountain paths — an offering that could be made by anyone who could pay a carver, which is why they line the old routes in their thousands.

Carving was categorised as one of the thirteen crafts in the seventeenth century, and it retained a particular prestige because it served scripture directly. Trashiyangtse and Thimphu remain its centres. The mask trade is now the commercial end of the craft, sustained partly by visitors, while block cutting has almost no market — printing moved on. HAB documents block-cutting technique for that reason: it is a craft with real historical weight and almost no economic reason left to exist.
crafts.long_description: Parzo is carving in three materials at once — wood, slate and stone — and each has its own discipline. In wood it produces the dance masks worn at tshechu, the choesham panels of a household altar, and the deep relief of a temple facade. In slate it produces the carved plaques set into mani walls. And in wood again, in reverse and in mirror image, it produces the printing blocks from which scripture was published for centuries before paper presses arrived. A block is cut in reverse and read in a mirror, so a single slip means starting the whole face again from new wood.
crafts.technique: Relief and in-the-round carving with chisels and adzes; mirror-cut for print blocks
crafts.materials: Seasoned walnut and maple, local slate, soapstone
crafts.typical_products: dance masks, altar panels, printing blocks, slate reliefs

crafts.name: Lhazo
crafts.description: Thangka scrolls, murals and decorative motifs painted to classical proportion in mineral pigment.
crafts.history:
Painting is the most codified of the thirteen. The proportions of a deity are set out in classical treatises brought from Tibet, and a painter begins not with a sketch but with a grid — laying down axes and unit measures before a single line is drawn. Get the iconometry wrong and the image is not merely poor, it is incorrect, which is a different order of failure.

Pigments were ground from mineral and earth: malachite for green, cinnabar for red, lapis for blue, orpiment for yellow, bound with hide glue. Gold was applied as leaf and burnished. Because the materials were expensive and the training long, thangka painters were commissioned rather than speculative, and a major scroll could occupy a studio for a year.

The craft also produced the murals covering temple interiors and the cloud, flower and jewel motifs running along the eaves of ordinary buildings — the decorative vocabulary most visitors read as simply Bhutanese.

Synthetic pigment and printed thangka have both arrived, and both undercut the mineral-painted scroll on price. HAB's position is that the distinction has to be made visible to buyers, which is why origin and materials are stated on every painted piece it sells.
crafts.long_description: Lhazo is painting governed by measurement. The proportions of a deity are set out in classical treatises, and a painter begins not with a sketch but with a grid, laying down the axes and unit measures before any line is drawn. Pigments are ground from mineral and earth — malachite, cinnabar, lapis, orpiment — and bound with hide glue. The same hand paints the scroll thangkas that hang in a shrine, the murals that cover a temple wall, and the cloud, flower and jewel motifs that run along a building’s eaves. The grid is laid before any line, because in this craft an image out of proportion is not merely poor but liturgically incorrect.
crafts.technique: Grid-set iconometry, mineral pigment bound in hide glue, brocade mounting
crafts.materials: Cotton canvas, mineral and earth pigments, gold leaf, silk brocade

crafts.name: Jinzo
crafts.description: Clay statues, ritual objects and moulded ornament, built up over a wooden armature.
crafts.history:
Clay and sculpture covers everything modelled rather than cut or cast. A statue begins as a wooden armature bound with cord, over which the sculptor builds up clay mixed with paper and cotton fibre so it dries without cracking. The finished figure is painted and gilded, and at that point it is indistinguishable from bronze to anyone who does not try to lift it.

That was the point. Bronze was expensive and had to be imported; clay was underfoot. A village temple that could not commission a cast image could commission a modelled one, and the same iconometric rules applied, so the object was liturgically identical. Much of what appears to be metal in Bhutanese temples is jinzo work.

The craft also produced small moulded offerings and the ornamental detail applied to walls and altars.

It is now among the most fragile of the thirteen. The commissions are religious and irregular, there is almost no consumer market, and the skill is held by a small number of practitioners concentrated around Thimphu, Punakha and Trongsa. Jinzo is one of the five crafts in HAB's skills transmission programme for exactly that reason.
crafts.long_description: Jinzo covers everything modelled rather than cut or cast. A statue begins as a wooden armature bound with cord, over which the sculptor builds up clay mixed with paper fibre and cotton so it will dry without cracking. The finished figure is painted and gilded, and at that point it is indistinguishable from bronze to anyone who does not lift it. The same craft produces the small moulded offerings and the ornamental detail applied to walls and altars. Fibre in the clay is what allows a figure to dry over weeks without splitting, and it is why modelled statues pass for cast bronze.
crafts.technique: Clay modelled over a bound wooden armature, fibre-reinforced, then painted and gilded
crafts.materials: Local clay, paper and cotton fibre, timber, pigment, gold leaf
crafts.shop_note: Sculpture is made to commission. Tell the secretariat what you have in mind and we will put a Jinzo member on it.

crafts.name: Lugzo
crafts.description: Casting in bronze, brass and iron — bells, statues, cymbals and household vessels.
crafts.history:
Casting is the lost-wax craft, and it destroys its own model. A figure is built in wax, coated in clay, then fired so the wax runs out and molten bronze takes its place — which means the mould must be broken to release the object, and no two castings are ever quite identical.

The trade produced the bells and cymbals used in ritual, statues large and small, and the heavy brass vessels that were once a household's most valuable possessions. Metal came in through trade with Tibet and India, and the casters worked where the patrons were.

It was always a small trade. A foundry needs charcoal, crucibles, a furnace and a great deal of fuel, and the capital required kept the number of workshops low. Skill passed within families.

Today cast statuary competes directly with imports from Nepal and India that are cheaper and often larger, and the domestic market cannot support many casters. Lugzo is in the skills transmission programme alongside Jinzo, Garzo, Dozo and Shingzo — the five crafts with the fewest practising members and the highest risk of a technique simply stopping.
crafts.long_description: Lugzo is the lost-wax craft. A model is built in wax, coated in clay, then fired so the wax runs out and molten bronze can take its place — which means the model is destroyed to make the object, and no two castings are ever quite identical. The trade produces the bells and cymbals used in ritual, statues large and small, and the heavy brass vessels that were once a household’s most valuable possessions. Because the mould must be broken to free the object, every casting is the only one of its kind, and a flaw cannot be corrected.
crafts.technique: Lost-wax casting; chased and polished after breaking the mould
crafts.shop_note: Cast work is made to order. Tell the secretariat what you need cast and we will match it to a Lugzo member.

crafts.name: Garzo
crafts.description: Forged tools, knives, chains and farm implements, a craft centred on eastern Bhutan.
crafts.history:
Blacksmithing is the craft the other twelve depend on. The chisel a carver uses, the adze a carpenter uses, the knife in every kitchen and the loom parts a weaver needs were all forged by a smith. Tradition attributes its introduction to a Tibetan saint in the fourteenth century, and the trade has been concentrated in the east — Trashigang and Mongar — ever since.

Its most visible legacy is the iron chain bridges: wrought links forged by hand and slung across gorges that could not otherwise be crossed. Sections survive, and they are the clearest demonstration of what the craft could do at scale.

A smith worked to a customer's hand rather than to a standard size, and a good knife was made once and resharpened for a lifetime. Charcoal forge, hand hammer, anvil, water quench — the toolkit has barely changed.

Imported steel tools have taken most of the market, and edged goods face export restrictions that close the visitor trade to smiths almost entirely. The result is a craft with real demand inside Bhutan, no export route, and a shrinking number of forges — which is why HAB's work here is domestic supply rather than market linkage.
crafts.long_description: Garzo is the working craft of the thirteen: it makes the things every other trade needs. Blacksmiths forge the chisels a carver uses, the adzes a carpenter uses, the knives a household uses, and the chains that once suspended iron bridges across the gorges of eastern Bhutan. The tradition is strongest in Trashigang and Mongar, and it is still normal for a smith to make a tool to a customer’s hand rather than to a standard size. A smith works to the customer’s hand rather than to a standard size, and a well-made blade is sharpened for a lifetime rather than replaced.
crafts.technique: Charcoal forge, hand hammer and anvil, water-quenched edges
crafts.materials: Wrought and tool steel, hardwood handles
crafts.shop_note: Edged tools face export restrictions. Write to the secretariat about buying direct in Bhutan from a Garzo member.

crafts.name: Troezo
crafts.description: Chased and filigreed silver and gold: koma clasps, jewellery, ritual vessels.
crafts.history:
Gold and silversmithing served two markets at once: the monastery and the household. For the monastery it produced ritual vessels, reliquaries and the silver mountings on ceremonial objects. For the household it produced jewellery and the koma — the pair of shoulder clasps that fasten a woman's kira, frequently the most valuable object a family owned and passed down through generations.

The characteristic techniques are chasing, where the surface is worked from the front with punches, and filigree, where drawn wire is soldered into open pattern. Both are slow and neither can be rushed convincingly, which is why a chased koma is still distinguishable from a cast copy at arm's length.

Silver came into Bhutan through trade with Tibet and India, and smiths clustered where that trade arrived and where patrons were — Thimphu and Trashiyangtse.

The modern problem is provenance. Cast and imported jewellery in Bhutanese forms is now widely sold to visitors, and a buyer has no way to tell. The Thimphu metalwork cluster's shared hallmark exists precisely for that: it lets a buyer identify Bhutanese hand-worked silver, and it is the model HAB would like extended to other crafts.
crafts.long_description: Troezo works precious metal at two scales. At the fine end it produces jewellery and the koma — the pair of shoulder clasps that fasten a woman’s kira, often the most valuable thing she owns and passed down through a family. At the larger end it produces ritual vessels, reliquaries and the silver mountings on ceremonial objects. The characteristic techniques are chasing, in which the surface is worked from the front with punches, and filigree, in which drawn wire is soldered into open pattern. Chasing is worked from the front with punches and cannot be hurried, which is why hand-worked silver still reads differently from a cast copy.
crafts.technique: Chasing and repoussé, drawn-wire filigree, granulation
crafts.typical_products: koma clasps, jewellery, ritual vessels, betel boxes

crafts.name: Tshazo
crafts.description: Split bamboo and cane woven into baskets, bangchungs, mats and quivers.
crafts.history:
Bamboo and cane work is the craft of the subtropical south and east, where the material grows. Zhemgang and the Kheng villages are its heartland, and the technique is held in families rather than in books — a weaver splits, dyes and weaves a piece from start to finish alone.

The defining object is the bangchung: a shallow lidded basket woven in two nesting halves, tight enough to hold cooked rice and, traditionally, water. It travelled with anyone going any distance, and its quality was judged by whether it leaked. Pattern is woven into the body in dyed strips rather than applied afterwards, so a bangchung's decoration and its structure are the same thing.

The craft also made floor mats, storage baskets, the conical rain hats worn in the east, and the quivers that carried arrows before archery became purely a sport.

When the road reached Zhemgang the market extended past the district almost overnight, and two things followed: demand began cutting bamboo faster than it regrew, and cheap imported baskets appeared sold as Kheng work. The cluster response — a common grading standard and replanted harvesting stands — is the clearest example in the sector of artisans regulating themselves.
crafts.long_description: Tshazo is woven from material the weaver harvests and splits by hand. The best-known object is the bangchung, a shallow lidded basket woven so tightly in two nesting halves that it will hold cooked rice and, traditionally, water. The craft also makes floor mats, storage baskets, the conical rain hats worn in the east, and the quivers that once carried arrows. Zhemgang and the Kheng region are its heartland, and the pattern work is done in dyed strips woven into the body rather than applied afterwards. Pattern is woven into the body in dyed strips, never applied afterwards, so a basket’s decoration and its structure are the same thing.
crafts.technique: Hand-split strips woven in twill and hexagonal patterns; two-part nesting lids
crafts.typical_products: bangchung baskets, mats, quivers, storage baskets

crafts.name: Thagzo
crafts.description: Backstrap and pedal-loom textiles — kira, gho, kisuthara silk and yathra wool.
crafts.history:
Weaving is the craft with the deepest reach into Bhutanese life and the strongest claim on its economy. Cloth was currency: taxes were paid in it, and a family's wealth could be read from the kira a woman wore at a festival. The most demanding textile, kisuthara, is patterned in supplementary weft, with the design built up thread by thread on a backstrap loom where the tension comes from the weaver's own body. A single kira can hold a weaver for eleven months, and nothing is written down.

Regional traditions are distinct. Lhuentse — Khoma in particular — is the centre of kisuthara silk. Bumthang weaves yathra, a heavy patterned wool for the cold, on pedal looms. Trashigang and Zhemgang have their own cotton and silk patterns. The differences are old enough to function as regional signatures.

Weaving is overwhelmingly women's work, and it remains the single largest source of craft income in rural Bhutan. That is also its exposure: imported machine-woven cloth in Bhutanese patterns now sells alongside handwoven work at a fraction of the price. Nearly every intervention HAB makes in weaving comes back to that problem — proving, at the point of sale, which is which.
crafts.long_description: Thagzo is the craft with the widest reach and the deepest prestige. Cloth is woven on a backstrap loom, where the tension comes from the weaver’s own body, or on a pedal loom for wider work. The most demanding textile is kisuthara, a silk kira patterned in supplementary weft where the design is built up thread by thread with no shortcut — a single length can take a year. In Bumthang the tradition is yathra, a heavy patterned wool woven for the cold. Weaving is overwhelmingly women’s work and remains the largest single source of craft income in rural Bhutan. Tension comes from the weaver’s own body against the loom, so no two weavers produce quite the same cloth from the same pattern.
crafts.technique: Backstrap and pedal looms; supplementary-weft patterning worked thread by thread
crafts.materials: Raw and reeled silk, cotton, sheep and yak wool, natural dyes
crafts.typical_products: kira and gho cloth, kisuthara silk, yathra wool, bags

crafts.name: Tshemzo
crafts.description: Tailoring, appliqué and embroidery, including the giant thongdrel banners.
crafts.history:
Tailoring and embroidery cover the smallest everyday objects and the largest religious ones. At one end the craft cuts and stitches gho and kira, boots and hats — work every household needed. At the other it produces the thongdrel, an appliqué banner several storeys high, assembled from cut and stitched silk, unfurled before dawn at a tshechu and rolled away before the sun can strike it. Merit is held to accrue simply from seeing one.

The technique is cut-silk appliqué rather than painting: shapes are cut from dyed silk and couched down with fine stitching, so the image is built from cloth. A thongdrel is a workshop project running to years, historically commissioned by a dzong or a wealthy patron, and its makers were named in the records.

Between those extremes sits embroidery on altar hangings, cushion covers and ceremonial dress. This is the part of the craft with the clearest contemporary market — appliqué cushion covers and bags sell readily to visitors and export buyers.

The risk is at the top end. Thongdrel commissions are rare, and the workshops able to execute one depend on them to keep the skill in practice at all.
crafts.long_description: Tshemzo runs from everyday tailoring to the largest religious objects made in Bhutan. At one end it is the cutting and stitching of gho and kira, boots and hats. At the other it is the thongdrel — an appliqué banner several storeys high, assembled from cut and stitched silk, unfurled before dawn at a tshechu and rolled away before the sun strikes it. The intermediate work is embroidery and appliqué on altar hangings, cushion covers and ceremonial dress. Shapes are cut from dyed silk and couched down with fine stitching, so the whole image is built from cloth rather than painted onto it.
crafts.technique: Cut-silk appliqué, couched and satin embroidery, hand-finished tailoring
crafts.materials: Raw silk, brocade, cotton, wool felt
crafts.typical_products: appliqué thongdrel, boots, cushion covers, bags

crafts.name: Shagzo
crafts.description: Bowls and cups turned from burl wood and lacquered, associated with healing properties.
crafts.history:
Wood turning belongs to Trashiyangtse, and has for centuries. The prized material is burl — the knotted, figured growth on a maple or rhododendron trunk, which cannot be planted or predicted, only found. It is turned green on a hand or treadle lathe, then dried slowly for months so it will not split, then lacquered.

The results are the dapa, a lidded serving bowl, and the phob, a cup carried on the person. Both were everyday objects and status objects at once: an ordinary phob was plain, and a finely figured one was a gift between officials. Certain woods were traditionally held to reveal poison and to carry healing properties, which is why the best phob were diplomatic presents rather than tableware.

The craft's constraint has always been supply rather than skill. Burl is scarce, and demand from visitors has pushed turners toward green-selling — turning and finishing wood that has not dried, which cracks within a year in a drier climate.

The Trashiyangtse cluster's shared drying store and turner's mark address both problems at once: wood is seasoned properly, and a buyer can see whose work it is.
crafts.long_description: Shagzo is turning, and Trashiyangtse is its centre. The prized material is burl — the knotted, figured growth on a maple or rhododendron trunk — which is turned green on a hand or treadle lathe, then dried slowly and finished with lacquer. The results are the dapa, a lidded serving bowl, and the phob, a cup carried on the person. Certain figured woods are traditionally held to have healing properties and to reveal poison, which is why the finest phob were diplomatic gifts. Burl is turned green and then dried for months, because wood finished wet will crack within a year in any drier climate.
crafts.technique: Green-turned on a hand or treadle lathe, slow-dried, lacquer finished
crafts.materials: Maple and rhododendron burl, natural lacquer
crafts.typical_products: dapa bowls, phob cups, lacquered containers

crafts.name: Dezo
crafts.description: Desho paper made by hand from daphne and edgeworthia bark, dried on frames in the sun.
crafts.history:
Paper making exists in Bhutan because scripture needed a surface. Desho is made from the bark of the daphne and edgeworthia shrubs, which is stripped, soaked, boiled with wood ash, beaten to a pulp, poured onto a screen and dried in the sun on its frame — which is why a sheet carries the faint texture of the mesh it was made on.

The paper's virtues are practical: it is naturally insect-resistant, it does not become brittle, and it lasts for centuries. Manuscripts on desho from the seventeenth century are still legible. Just as importantly, daphne coppices — cut it and it regrows — so harvesting a stand does not destroy it, and a paper-making village can work the same hillside indefinitely.

Punakha is the best-known centre, and the craft was for most of its history a monastic supply trade rather than a commercial one.

Printing moved to industrial paper, which removed the original market entirely. What replaced it is stationery, gift wrap, lampshades and notebooks sold largely to visitors — a smaller but genuine market, and one of the few crafts where the environmental case and the commercial case point the same way.
crafts.long_description: Dezo makes desho, the paper Bhutanese scripture was written on. The bark of the daphne and edgeworthia shrubs is stripped, soaked, boiled with ash, beaten to a pulp and poured onto a screen, then dried in the sun on its frame — which is why a sheet of desho carries the faint texture of the mesh it was made on. The paper is naturally insect-resistant and lasts for centuries, and the plants coppice, so harvesting them does not kill the stand. The pulp is poured rather than dipped and dried on its frame in the sun, which is why each sheet carries the texture of its mesh.
crafts.technique: Bark cooked with ash, hand-beaten to pulp, poured and sun-dried on frames
crafts.materials: Daphne bhola and edgeworthia bark, wood ash
crafts.typical_products: desho sheets, notebooks, envelopes, gift wrap

outlets.description: The only authentic crafts market validated and managed by HAB. Every stall is a registered member selling their own work, priced as agreed with the association — no resellers, no imported copies.
outlets.long_description: The market was set up so that visitors arriving in Punakha could buy directly from the people who make the work, at a price the maker agreed to. Stalls are allocated to registered members by rotation, so weavers from Lhuentse and bamboo workers from Zhemgang trade alongside Punakha’s own paper makers rather than competing with a permanent shop. HAB staff verify every seller’s membership and craft category, check that nothing on a stall was imported for resale, and hold the price list that stallholders agreed at the start of the season. Demonstrations run through the afternoon, and the association can arrange a weaving or paper-making session for a group with notice.

clusters.name: Khoma Weaving Cluster
clusters.summary: Forty-two women weaving kisuthara silk on backstrap looms, in the village the textile is named for.
clusters.story: Khoma sits above the Kuri Chhu, an hour’s walk from the road when the cluster was formed. Almost every household here weaves, and the village gives its name to the kisuthara patterns that are the most demanding silk work in Bhutan — a single kira can hold a weaver for eleven months, the design built up thread by thread in supplementary weft with nothing written down. Before the cluster existed, buyers came up from the valley and set the price, and a weaver had no way to know what her work sold for in Thimphu. Forty-two weavers now hold a common price list, buy reeled silk together at a rate none of them could get alone, and take turns travelling down to the trade fairs. The youngest member joined at nineteen; the eldest has been weaving for fifty-one years and taught eleven of the others.
clusters.visitor_note: Weavers receive visitors most mornings. Arrange through the HAB secretariat.

clusters.name: Kheng Bamboo Cluster
clusters.summary: Bamboo and cane workers across the Kheng villages, making bangchung baskets to a technique held locally.
clusters.story: The Kheng region grows the bamboo and works it where it stands. A bangchung — the shallow lidded basket woven in two nesting halves — is split, dyed and woven by one person from start to finish, and the twill patterns are held in families rather than in books. The cluster formed when the road reached Zhemgang and the market suddenly extended past the district: thirty-six households agreed a grading standard so that a basket sold as Kheng work would hold water as it should, and agreed not to undercut each other on it. They now supply the association’s outlets, the Punakha market and, since 2024, two retailers abroad. The cluster also replanted harvesting stands, because the demand that arrived with the road was cutting bamboo faster than it grew back.
clusters.visitor_note: Demonstrations at the cluster shed, Trong. Half a day from Zhemgang town.

clusters.name: Trashiyangtse Turning Cluster
clusters.summary: The country’s wood-turning centre — dapa bowls and phob cups turned from burl and lacquered.
clusters.story: Trashiyangtse is where Bhutanese turning is from. The lathes here are worked by hand or treadle, and the material is burl: the knotted growth on a maple or rhododendron trunk, which is turned while still green, then dried slowly for months so it will not split, then lacquered. Certain figured woods are traditionally held to reveal poison, which is why the finest phob cups were given as diplomatic gifts. The cluster’s problem was never skill but supply — burl cannot be planted, only found — so the twenty-four turners agreed a sourcing protocol with the forestry office, took on a shared drying store so wood could be seasoned properly instead of sold green, and began marking each piece with the turner’s name. That mark is now what distinguishes their work from imported bowls sold as Bhutanese.
clusters.visitor_note: The cluster workshop is in Trashiyangtse town, near the chorten.

clusters.name: Chumey Yathra Cluster
clusters.summary: Yathra wool weaving along the Chumey valley — blankets, jackets and saddle bags.
clusters.story: Yathra is woven for the cold, in heavy patterned wool on pedal looms, and the Chumey valley has made it for as long as anyone records. Thirty-one weavers now share dyeing facilities and a common wool purchase, and have moved from selling blankets at the roadside to supplying finished garments and bags.

clusters.name: Jungshi Paper Cluster
clusters.summary: Desho paper makers working daphne and edgeworthia bark by hand.
clusters.story: Desho paper is made by stripping, cooking and beating shrub bark, then pouring the pulp onto frames to dry in the sun. Eighteen makers work here, and because daphne coppices, harvesting does not kill the stand — the cluster manages its own harvesting rotation.

clusters.name: Thimphu Metalwork Cluster
clusters.summary: Silversmiths and casters working koma clasps, jewellery and ritual vessels.
clusters.story: Twenty-seven silversmiths and casters share premises and a hallmark in Thimphu, working chased silver, drawn-wire filigree and lost-wax bronze. The shared hallmark was the point: it lets a buyer tell a Bhutanese-made koma from an import.

news.title: Trade facilitation desk opens for the autumn export season
news.blurb: Members can now book one-to-one sessions on export documentation, EMS rates and commercial invoicing at the HAB office in Thimphu.
news.body:
The trade facilitation desk is open at the HAB office on Metog Lam from 1 September to the end of November, the months in which most member consignments leave the country. Members book a forty-minute session and bring a real order rather than a hypothetical one.

The desk covers the paperwork a shipment needs and the order in which it has to be assembled: the commercial invoice and its valuation, the certificate of origin, the customs declaration for the destination market, and the craft certificate HAB issues with every parcel. Officers also compare EMS and courier rates against the weight and declared value of the consignment, which for small parcels is where most of the avoidable cost sits.

Two questions came up repeatedly last season and are dealt with directly. The first is valuation — members have been declaring the retail price rather than the transaction value, and paying duty accordingly at the far end. The second is consolidation. Where several members in the same dzongkhag are sending to the same market, the secretariat will now pool the parcels into one shipment through Thimphu, at a cost per piece that is a fraction of what each would pay alone.

Sessions are open to Active Sector Members and are booked by telephone or email. Members who cannot travel to Thimphu can send scanned documents in advance and take the session by telephone. The desk will publish a short summary of common errors at the end of the season.

news.title: Natural dye training concludes in Lhuentse
news.blurb: Twenty-six weavers from Khoma and Gangzur completed a ten-day course on madder, indigo and lac dye preparation.
news.body:
Twenty-six weavers from Khoma and Gangzur completed a ten-day residential course in natural dyeing this month, run with the Khoma cluster under the resource-efficiency project.

The course was built around a problem the cluster had raised itself. Madder, indigo and lac have largely given way to synthetic dye on grounds of cost and, more importantly, consistency: a weaver taking a commission cannot risk a batch that comes out a different colour from the last. The training therefore concentrated less on the dyes themselves than on making the process repeatable — mordanting, water quality, ratios by weight rather than by eye, timings, and a written batch record for every pot.

Participants dyed and recorded eleven batches each. Colour-fastness was tested at the end of the course by washing and sun exposure, and the results were logged against the recipe so a weaver can see which of their own batches held and which did not. Each participant left with a sample card, their batch book, and enough prepared madder and lac to complete one commission.

The course was taught by two master weavers from the cluster with a technical officer from the secretariat. Places were allocated to Active Sector Members practising Thagzo, with priority to first-time participants; materials and accommodation were covered by the project and travel was not.

The next intake runs from 4 November, again at Khoma, with twenty-six places. Applications open through the Membership Services officer six weeks in advance.

news.title: Zorig Chusum craft bazaar returns to Clock Tower Square
news.blurb: Forty member enterprises will exhibit across three days, with live demonstrations from each of the thirteen crafts.
news.body:
The Zorig Chusum craft bazaar returns to Clock Tower Square in Thimphu from 12 September, running three days from nine in the morning to six in the evening. Entry is free.

Forty member enterprises take stalls, arranged by craft so that a visitor can walk the thirteen disciplines in sequence rather than hunting for them. Demonstrations run continuously through each afternoon: backstrap weaving, bamboo splitting, paper pouring, lathe turning and blacksmithing, with the maker at work and the finished piece alongside.

Members sell directly and keep the proceeds. Prices are those agreed with the association, which is to say the same price the piece carries in the HAB outlet, so a visitor is not choosing between the bazaar and the shop on cost. Every stallholder is a registered member selling their own work; there are no resellers and no imported stock.

The bazaar is the association’s largest public event of the year and its main recruiting ground. Membership Services will hold a desk at the north end of the square for artisans who want to apply, and the trade facilitation desk will run sessions for members who have export orders in hand.

Stalls are allocated by the secretariat. Applications from Active Sector Members close four weeks before the opening, and priority goes to enterprises that have not exhibited in the previous cycle and to the crafts with the fewest practising members. Write to the office to be added to the list.

news.title: Annual report 2025 available to download
news.blurb: Sector figures, programme outcomes and audited accounts for the year, published in English and Dzongkha.
news.body:
The annual report for 2025 is published and free to download from the publications library, in English and Dzongkha, alongside the audited financial statements for the same year.

The report sets out what the association did against the objects in the Articles of Association and what it cost. It carries the sector figures the secretariat maintains — the network of 7,500 micro and small enterprises, 5,250 of them women-led, and 195 affiliated stores — together with programme outcomes for the year, the project portfolio, and the membership and governance record.

Three results are reported at length. Cleaner-production audits reached 240 workshops across nine dzongkhags and cut measured waste by an average of 31 percent. Four hundred products were photographed and catalogued to export standard, and export documentation clinics ran in six dzongkhags. Forty paid two-year apprenticeships were opened in the five crafts with the fewest practising masters.

The audited statements are prepared by an independent auditor and presented in the format required under the Civil Society Organizations Act. They are received by the Annual Sector Forum together with the report, which is where members put questions to the Board of Trustees on both.

Members who would prefer a printed copy can collect one from the office on Metog Lam or ask for it at a Dzongkhag Chapter meeting. Earlier reports back to 2018 are in the same library, as are the audited accounts for each year.

news.title: Product innovation lab pairs six artisans with designers
news.blurb: A six-month cycle developing new homeware lines from bamboo, yathra and desho paper for international retail.
news.body:
Six member artisans have been paired with product designers for a six-month development cycle, working on homeware lines in bamboo, yathra and desho paper for international retail.

The pairings answer a specific gap. Members reach buyers with pieces made for a domestic or ceremonial use, and buyers ask for something in the same technique at a size, price and function their own market recognises. Neither side is well placed to bridge that alone: the designer does not know what the material will do, and the artisan has no reason to guess at a foreign kitchen shelf.

Each pair works to a brief agreed at the start — a defined product family, a target landed price, and a production method the artisan can repeat without new equipment. The cycle runs in three stages: technique and material study, prototyping with costed bills of material, and a sampling run of twenty pieces that goes in front of buyers at the November inbound mission.

Intellectual property in the resulting designs rests with the artisan. Where a line goes into production, the designer is paid a fee from project funds rather than a royalty, so the member is not carrying a permanent cost on their own product.

The six crafts represented are Thagzo, Tshazo, Dezo, Shagzo, Lhadri and Garzo. Outcomes, costings and what failed will be published as a case study at the end of the cycle so the method can be repeated without the project.

events.title: Zorig Chusum craft bazaar
events.summary: Forty member enterprises exhibit across three days, with live demonstrations from each of the thirteen crafts.
events.detail:
The bazaar is the association’s largest public event of the year. Forty member enterprises take stalls in Clock Tower Square, arranged by craft so a visitor can walk the thirteen disciplines in sequence rather than hunting for them.

Demonstrations run continuously through each afternoon — backstrap weaving, bamboo splitting, paper pouring, lathe turning and blacksmithing — with the maker at work and the finished piece alongside. Members sell directly and keep the proceeds. Prices are those agreed with the association, the same price the piece carries in the HAB outlet, so a visitor is not choosing between the bazaar and the shop on cost. Every stallholder is a registered member selling their own work: no resellers, no imported stock.

Entry is free and the square stays open from nine to six on all three days. The busiest hours are late morning and the two hours before closing; the demonstrations are quietest, and easiest to watch properly, in the early afternoon.

Membership Services holds a desk at the north end of the square for artisans who want to apply to join, and the trade facilitation desk runs sessions for members with export orders in hand. Both are staffed for the full three days.

Stalls are allocated by the secretariat. Applications from Active Sector Members close four weeks before the opening. Priority goes to enterprises that did not exhibit in the previous cycle and to the crafts with the fewest practising members. Stallholders are asked to bring their own display and to price every piece visibly before the doors open.

events.title: Export documentation clinic
events.summary: One-to-one sessions on export paperwork, EMS rates and commercial invoicing.
events.detail:
Members bring an actual consignment and leave with the paperwork completed. The clinic is not a lecture: an officer works through one member’s order at a time, with the documents on the table.

The session covers the commercial invoice and how the transaction value is arrived at, the certificate of origin, the customs declaration for the destination market, and the craft certificate HAB issues with every parcel. Officers compare EMS and courier rates against the weight and declared value of the consignment, which for small parcels is where most of the avoidable cost sits.

Two errors account for most of the problems seen last season. The first is declaring the retail price rather than the transaction value, which leaves the buyer paying duty on a figure the member never received. The second is sending alone: where several members in the same dzongkhag are shipping to the same market, the secretariat will consolidate the parcels into one shipment through Thimphu at a fraction of the per-piece cost.

Sessions run forty minutes and must be booked in advance. Bring the order, the buyer’s details, the weight of the packed consignment, and your member number. Members who cannot travel to Thimphu can send scanned documents ahead and take the session by telephone.

The desk is open to Active Sector Members from September to the end of November, and a summary of common errors is published to the membership at the end of the season.

events.title: Annual Sector Forum
events.summary: The annual meeting of the sector membership: annual report, audited accounts and sector consultation.
events.detail:
Under the Articles of Association the Annual Sector Forum receives the annual report and audited accounts, considers the strategic direction, and provides the forum for sector-wide consultation.

The morning is given to the report and the accounts. The Board of Trustees presents both, the independent auditor takes questions on the statements, and the Forum records its receipt of them. The afternoon is consultation: the strategic plan is reviewed against what the year actually delivered, and the Dzongkhag Chapters bring the matters raised at their own meetings — raw material supply, pricing, and the crafts where practising numbers are still falling.

Active Sector Members hold a vote. Associate members attend and are consulted but do not vote. Honorary members hold a standing invitation. Members of the secretariat attend to answer on delivery rather than to speak for the Board.

Papers are circulated to the membership two weeks in advance: the annual report, the audited statements, the workplan and budget for the coming year, and any resolution put by the Board or by a Chapter. A member wanting an item taken at the Forum should send it to the secretariat before the papers go out, in writing, with the support of one other Active member.

The Forum is where the association’s accountability to its own membership is discharged, and attendance is recorded. Travel support is available to Chapter representatives from the eastern dzongkhags on application to the office.

events.title: Natural dye training, Lhuentse
events.summary: Madder, indigo and lac dye preparation for weavers, run with the Khoma cluster.
events.detail:
A ten-day residential course at Khoma covering the preparation of madder, indigo and lac dyes, mordanting, colour-fastness testing and batch record keeping.

The course concentrates less on the dyes than on making the process repeatable. A weaver taking a commission cannot risk a batch that comes out a different colour from the last, and that risk — not cost alone — is why synthetic dye displaced the traditional preparations. Participants therefore work by weight rather than by eye, record water quality, ratios and timings for every pot, and keep a written batch book they take away with them.

Each participant dyes and records eleven batches. Colour-fastness is tested at the end of the course by washing and sun exposure, and results are logged against the recipe, so a weaver can see which of their own batches held and which did not. Everyone leaves with a sample card, their batch book, and enough prepared madder and lac to complete one commission.

Teaching is by two master weavers from the Khoma cluster with a technical officer from the secretariat. Places are allocated to Active Sector Members practising Thagzo, with priority to cluster members and first-time participants.

Materials and accommodation are covered by the project; travel is not. Twenty-six places. Applications open through the Membership Services officer six weeks before the start and close when the intake is full.

events.title: Inbound buyer mission
events.summary: Retail buyers from India, Thailand and Japan meet member enterprises.
events.detail:
Fourteen retail and wholesale buyers from India, Thailand and Japan visit Thimphu under the Market Access project. The mission is a working day, not a reception.

Member enterprises with export-ready product and completed catalogue photography are matched to buyers in advance on what each buyer has said they are looking for. Matched members get a scheduled thirty-minute meeting; walk-in members can join the open session after 14:00, when buyers move through the room by craft.

Bring physical samples, a price list in USD, your minimum order quantity, and a lead time you can hold. Buyers will ask all four in the first five minutes, and an answer of “it depends” generally ends the conversation. Members who came to the last mission without a price list are strongly advised to attend the costing workshop the week before.

The secretariat sits in on scheduled meetings only where a member asks it to, and follows up every introduction in writing within a week so that nothing rests on a verbal indication. Sample shipping after the mission is consolidated through the office.

Open to Craft Enterprise members and to producer groups nominated by a Dzongkhag Chapter. Registration closes two weeks before, and matched members are notified with their buyer’s brief five days in advance. Fourteen buyers, roughly forty scheduled meetings, one afternoon — the constraint is time, so preparation decides what comes of it.

events.title: Apprenticeship intake briefing
events.summary: Briefing for young artisans applying to the master-to-apprentice placements.
events.detail:
The Skills Transmission project opens forty paid two-year placements across the five crafts with the fewest practising members — Lugzo, Garzo, Jinzo, Dozo and Shingzo. This briefing is for young artisans considering an application, and for parents who want to understand what the two years involve.

These five crafts share a pattern. The work is commissioned rather than sold, the commissions are irregular, and a young person cannot afford years of unpaid apprenticeship. The placements address the money rather than the sentiment: the apprentice is paid a monthly stipend for the full two years, and the master is paid for teaching.

The briefing covers eligibility, the stipend and what it does and does not cover, the working week, how masters and apprentices are matched, and what happens at the end — including the tools grant and the route into membership as an Active Sector Member.

Eighteen masters are taking apprentices this cycle. Matching is done on craft, location and the master’s own assessment, and both sides meet before a placement is confirmed. Technique is documented in video and print as it is taught, and the curriculum developed with each master is shared with the Institute of Zorig Chusum.

Open to applicants aged 16–30. No prior training is required and no fee is charged. Applications close six weeks after the briefing; the form is available at the office and through Dzongkhag Chapters.

about.intro: Handicrafts Association of Bhutan (HAB) was established in 2005 and got formally registered as Civil Society Organization in 2011 under the CSO act of Bhutan 2007 as a pioneer centre for the promotion of vibrant and sustainable Bhutanese handicrafts.

vision.title: Towards a vibrant & sustainable handicrafts sector
vision.body: A Bhutan where the thirteen crafts remain in daily practice, and where making them is a livelihood a young person would choose.

mission.title: Promoting sustainability, inclusiveness and resilience
mission.body: HAB supports local artisans by providing resources, training and policy interventions to improve their skills and increase their chances of success in local communities and the tourism industry.

objectives: Improve market access for Bhutanese artisans at home, in the tourism sector and internationally.
Raise product quality and consistency through training, standards and inspection.
Guarantee fair compensation and prompt payment for handcrafted work.
Keep the thirteen crafts of Zorig Chusum in living practice, particularly those with few practitioners.
Represent the sector in policy dialogue with government and development partners.
Strengthen member enterprises as businesses — costing, licensing, export documentation and finance.

values.title: Care
values.body: Care for the maker, the material and the object. We do not ask an artisan to cut a corner we would not put our own name to, and we do not sell work we have not handled.

values.title: Respect
values.body: Respect for a tradition older than the association, and for the person who carries it. Masters are consulted, not instructed; technique is recorded on the maker’s terms.

values.title: Attentive
values.body: Attentive to quality, to the market and to what members actually ask for. Programmes are designed from what artisans report, and are dropped when they stop working.

values.title: Fair
values.body: Fair dealing, in writing. Prices are agreed with the maker and paid upfront, consignment risk stays with the association, and no member is undercut by another.

values.title: Transparent
values.body: Transparent about money and results. Audited accounts, programme outcomes and project evaluations are published every year in English and Dzongkha.

about.governance_note: HAB is a Public Benefit Organisation under the Civil Society Organizations Act of Bhutan 2007, as amended in 2022. Authority runs from the sector membership upward: the Annual Sector Forum receives the accounts and the Board of Trustees is accountable for governance, with Dzongkhag Chapters carrying representation into all twenty districts.

governance.note: Artisans, producers, designers, traders and service providers across the handicrafts value chain, admitted as Active or Affiliated members. Active Sector Members receive preferential access to services.
The annual meeting of the sector membership. Receives the annual report and audited accounts, considers the strategic direction, and provides the forum for sector-wide consultation.

Holds fiduciary responsibility for HAB and is accountable to the Authority for compliance. Adopts the Strategic Plan and approves annual workplans and budgets; may resolve that further activity falls within the objects.
Subnational structures carrying representation and service delivery into all twenty dzongkhags, so rural and informal producers participate on equal terms.
Delivers the approved workplan under the Board, maintains the statutory registers and records, and files reports and returns to the Authority under BCAS.
Held for the long-term financial sustainability of the sector, alongside grants, donations and project funding administered under the Board.

membershipCategories.name: Individual Artisan
membershipCategories.tagline: A craftsperson working on their own or with family.
membershipCategories.meaning: The core membership of the association. It is for the person who actually makes the work — a weaver at her own loom, a turner at his own lathe — whether or not the household is formally registered as a business. HAB was founded to represent this member, and Active status carries full participation: a vote at the Annual Sector Forum, a listing in the public directory, and first call on training places.
criteria: Bhutanese citizen holding a valid Citizenship Identity Card
Practising one or more of the thirteen crafts of Zorig Chusum
Able to demonstrate craft skill, by sample or by reference from a member
No business licence required — informal and household producers qualify
how: Complete the online application and choose Individual Artisan.
Select your primary craft and dzongkhag.
Upload your Citizenship Identity Card.
Pay the annual dues by card, mBoB or bank transfer.
The secretariat verifies your documents within five working days.
benefits: Listing in the public membership database, searchable by craft and dzongkhag
Preferential access to skills training and natural dye courses
Consignment of work to the HAB shop, bought at an agreed price and paid upfront
A stall by rotation at Punakha Crafts Market and the craft bazaars
Participation in your Dzongkhag Chapter
A vote at the Annual Sector Forum
membershipCategories.note: Roughly seventy percent of the association’s network is women-led. Dues may be waived by the Board in cases of hardship.

membershipCategories.name: Craft Enterprise
membershipCategories.tagline: Registered workshops, producer groups and cooperatives.
membershipCategories.meaning: For the member that employs or organises other artisans — a workshop with staff, a village producer group, a registered cooperative. The category exists because these members carry different obligations and different needs: they buy raw material in volume, they take wholesale orders, and they need export documentation. Active status is the same as for an individual artisan; the services are scaled to a business.
criteria: Registered in Bhutan as a business, cooperative or producer group
Producing in one or more of the thirteen crafts
At least two working members or employees
Valid business licence, or a gewog-issued group registration
how: Complete the online application and choose Craft Enterprise.
Select your primary craft and dzongkhag.
Upload your business licence or group registration.
Pay the annual dues by card, mBoB or bank transfer.
The secretariat verifies your documents within five working days.
benefits: Everything an Individual Artisan receives
Wholesale and buyer leads through the trade facilitation desk
Allocated slots at domestic and international trade fairs
Export documentation support and consolidated EMS shipping
Access to project-funded business training and green business planning
Eligibility for the revolving raw-material fund where a project supports it
membershipCategories.note: Enterprises with more than twenty employees are admitted at the same fee; the Board may set a separate class if the sector requires it.

membershipCategories.name: Artisan Cluster
membershipCategories.fee_note: per year for the cluster, renewable each July
membershipCategories.tagline: A village or valley organising around one craft.
membershipCategories.meaning: A cluster joins as a body rather than as individuals. It exists where a craft is concentrated in one place and the people making it have agreed to act together — a common price list, materials bought in bulk, a shared grading standard, sometimes a shared mark. One membership covers the whole cluster, which is cheaper than every household joining separately and gives the group a single voice in its Dzongkhag Chapter. Individual members may still hold their own Individual Artisan membership alongside it.
criteria: At least ten artisans working the same craft in one gewog or valley
A named representative authorised to act for the cluster
An agreed common price list or grading standard
A member list with names and Citizenship ID numbers
Formal group registration is welcome but not required
how: Agree at a cluster meeting to apply, and name a representative.
Complete the online registration and choose Artisan cluster.
Give the cluster name, area, total members and the crafts practised.
Upload the member list and any group registration certificate.
Pay the annual dues; the secretariat may visit before approval.
benefits: One membership covering every artisan in the cluster
A cluster page on the HAB website telling your story, with photographs
Visitors routed to you through the outlets and clusters section
Bulk raw-material purchase and shared-facility support
Priority in project-funded training delivered on site
A single voice in your Dzongkhag Chapter and at the Annual Sector Forum
membershipCategories.note: Clusters are visited by the secretariat before approval, to confirm the member list and the common price list. Six clusters are currently registered.

membershipCategories.name: Affiliated Member
membershipCategories.tagline: Retailers, hotels, schools and partner organisations.
membershipCategories.meaning: For organisations that work with the sector without producing craft themselves — a hotel that buys for its rooms, a retailer that stocks member work, a school that teaches Zorig Chusum, a development partner that funds a project. Associate members receive general sector benefits and are consulted, but they do not vote: the association is governed by the people who make the work.
criteria: A legally constituted organisation, in Bhutan or abroad
A demonstrable interest in the Bhutanese handicrafts sector
Agreement to the association’s code of conduct on authenticity and fair dealing
No craft production requirement
how: Complete the online application and choose Affiliated Member.
Give your organisation’s registration details and a contact person.
State your interest in the sector — buyer, educator, partner or funder.
Pay the annual dues by card, bank transfer or invoice.
The Board considers affiliated-member applications at its next sitting.
benefits: Listing in the public directory as an affiliated member of the association
Sector data, market intelligence briefs and all publications
Invitation to policy consultations and the Annual Sector Forum
Introductions to Active members producing in the crafts you buy
Use of the association’s authenticity guidance for your own sourcing
membershipCategories.note: Affiliated Members do not hold a vote and are not eligible for Board of Trustees positions.

membershipCategories.name: Honorary Member
membershipCategories.tagline: Master craftspeople and long-standing contributors to the sector.
membershipCategories.meaning: Conferred by resolution of the Board of Trustees on a master craftsperson, a retired member, or a person who has given long service to Bhutanese handicrafts. It carries the standing of Active membership without dues, and is the association’s way of keeping master practitioners in the network after they stop trading.
criteria: Recognised mastery of a Zorig Chusum craft, or long service to the sector
Nomination by two Active Sector Members or by a Dzongkhag Chapter
Resolution of the Board of Trustees
how: Honorary membership cannot be applied for.
Any two Active members, or a Dzongkhag Chapter, may submit a nomination to the secretariat.
The Board considers nominations annually before the Sector Forum.
Conferral is announced at the Annual Sector Forum.
benefits: All Active Sector Member benefits, with no annual dues
Standing invitation to the Annual Sector Forum
Priority as a master in the skills transmission programme
Recognition in the public directory and the annual report
membershipCategories.note: Honorary membership is held for life unless withdrawn by the Board.
